title: VB9-03939
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Mexico.

The Appellant claims refugee protection as a member of a particular social group, being a woman subject to gender-based persecution. She fears that her estranged husband, XXXX, will harm her if she returns to her native Mexico.
The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Merida, Mexico.
The Appellant argues on appeal that her estranged husband will be able to locate and harm her in the IFA.

The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida, Mexico. I find that the RPD did not err. I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida, Mexico.
I dismiss this appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.
The Appellant has been in Canada since XXXX 2008. She met her estranged husband, a Canadian citizen, in XXXX 2016 and married him in XXXX 2016. Their daughter was born in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The Appellant testified that her estranged husband had problems with drinking and drugs and that he became an abusive spouse. The couple split in XXXX 2017 when the husband returned to Quebec and the Appellant remained in British Columbia (BC).

Subsequent to the RPD decision dated April 29, 2019, the Appellant filed for divorce in BC in XXXX 2019. The Appellant has asked the BC Court to grant her sole custody of her daughter, and to award child support and spousal support.
The Appellant testified that she was threatened by her estranged husband and by his father who resides in Mexico and has connections to organized crime.
The Appellant says she is afraid to go back to Mexico because she believes that her estranged husband would act on threats against her if she was in Mexico.
The Minister has intervened in this case asking that the RAD uphold the RPD decision that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Minister argues that the new evidence submitted by the Appellant at perfection should not be admitted because it does not meet the criteria as set out in Raza.2 The Minister argues that that the Appellant's new evidence is not material or relevant to the contested issues and does not disprove a fact that was not known to the RPD at the time of the hearing.

The Minister further argues that the onus is on the Appellant to prove that she does not have an IFA. The Minister argues that the case law submitted by the Appellant is not relevant to the present case.
I will consider the Minister's arguments in the analysis that follows. NEW EVIDENCE Evidence presented by the Appellant at perfection is accepted

The Appellant seeks to introduce the following into evidence: a. Letter from XXXX XXXX, Barrister and Solicitor, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. b. Notice of Family Claim filed in the Supreme Court of British Columbia on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019.

According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or, iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.4
I find that the new evidence arose after the RPD decision dated April 29, 2019.

I find that the evidence is new and relevant in that it provides additional information regarding the current relationship between the Appellant and her estranged husband. This information is credible in that it comes from a BC solicitor and barrister. The information is relevant to the determinative issue because it addresses the future ability of her estranged husband to locate the Appellant and their daughter in the IFA.

The Appellant has not requested a hearing under 110(6) of IRPA. I will not convene a hearing. Submission in Response to Minister's Intervention is Accepted, Evidence Submitted After Perfection is Not Accepted (RAD Rule 29)5

In a submission dated July 16, 2020, the Appellant seeks to introduce the following into evidence: a. Response to Minister; b. A letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; c. An Application for child care benefits - special needs child; and, d. Paternity test results
In a submission dated August 31, 2020, the Appellant seeks to introduce the following into evidence: a. A letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXices

In deciding whether to allow an application for late submissions or late evidence, I must consider any relevant factors, including: a) the document's relevance and probative value; b) any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and, c) whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with the appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record

I find that the Appellant's submission in response to the Minister's submission is admitted to the extent that it provides the Appellant's response to the Minister's arguments with respect to the determinative issue of IFA.

The documents submitted by the Appellant as late evidence are not admitted. The Appellant has not provided a detailed submission as required by the RAD Rules regarding the admissibility of the proposed documentary evidence: two letters from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, an application for childcare benefits, and paternity test results. The Appellant has not explained what new evidence these documents bring to the appeal and the relevance and probative value of the new evidence.

There is evidence already before me regarding the counselling and mental health support that the Appellant has received in Canada. I have allowed new evidence submitted at perfection regarding the Appellant's family law proceedings.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.6

Sworn testimony before the Immigration and Refugee Board is presumed to be true unless the presumption of truth has been rebutted. The presumption of truth does not extend to conclusions or assumptions that a witness might put forward in testimony. 7

The RPD found that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida, Mexico. The RPD canvassed Merida as an IFA at the RPD hearing and received post-hearing submissions from Appellant's Counsel and the Minister on this issue.
The Appellant challenges the correctness of the RPD's IFA analysis.

The key concepts concerning IFA come from two cases.8 The adjudicating panel must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that: i. there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted or, on the balance of probabilities, subjected to a risk to life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the IFA and, ii. that conditions in that part of the country are such that it would be reasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for her to seek refuge there

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant's estranged husband or his father did not have the means or motivation to pursue her in Merida. The Appellant argues further that the RPD erred in finding that it was reasonable for the Appellant to seek refuge in Merida.

I find that the RPD did not err. I have conducted my own independent analysis of the evidence and the testimony and I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Merida for the reasons that follow. Her Estranged Husband Will Know the Appellant's Whereabouts

The Appellant argues on appeal that her estranged husband will now be able to locate her in Mexico because of Family Law proceedings that the Appellant has initiated in the Supreme Court of British Columbia (the BC Court). The Appellant has adduced new evidence that she has asked the BC Court to grant her a divorce, to award her sole custody of their daughter, and to order her estranged husband to make spousal support and child support payments to the Appellant.

The BC Court proceedings will require that the Appellant and her estranged husband exchange documents before, during and after the resolution of the case. The Appellant introduced, as new evidence at the RAD, a letter from her Family Law attorney stating that it is rare for BC Courts to grant sole custody to a parent, and that it is likely that the Appellant will be required to maintain some level of contact with her estranged husband if they share custody of their child, Victoria, or if the BC Court grants her estranged husband visiting rights.

The BC Court will order such support and access as it deems appropriate in the circumstances of this action having due regard for the well-being of all parties. The Appellant will have the opportunity to bring to the attention of the BC Court any concerns she may have about her estranged husband's future access to their child and to herself.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its analysis of the Appellant's estranged husband's ability to find her in Mexico. Given subsequent developments in the case and the new evidence that the Appellant has adduced at the RAD, the RPD's analysis is no longer relevant. I find that, given the Family Law proceedings initiated by the Appellant, it is more likely than not that the Appellant's estranged husband will be able to locate her in Mexico in the future.
I have no evidence before me that the Appellant's petition for divorce has been decided by the BC Court. Possibility of Persecution in Merida

The RPD found that the Appellant's estranged husband, or his father, would not have the means or the will to contact and harm the Appellant in Mexico.9 The Appellant argues on appeal that the agents of persecution will have the means to locate the Appellant in Mexico. Given the new evidence, I have found that the Appellant's estranged husband will be able to locate her in Mexico. In order for her to be at risk however, the agents of persecution must have both the means and the will to harm the Appellant.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in speculating that the agents of persecution will not be motivated to harm the Appellant. The Appellant cites Sanchez v. Canada10 as a case, with similar facts to the present case, to support an argument that the RPD erred by speculating and reaching a finding not supported by the evidence.
I find the RPD did not err. I find that the facts in Sanchez v. Canada differ significantly from the facts in the present case.

In Sanchez v. Canada, the family in question had already had their property expropriated by the criminals targeting them. The Federal Court found that it was speculative for the RPD to conclude the family would not be targeted further. This is not the fact pattern in the present case. In the present case, the Appellant has suffered domestic abuse at the hands of her husband in the past, however there is no evidence that she has been targeted by organized criminal organizations or that she has suffered further physical abuse from her husband once their relationship ended.

The Appellant testified that she fears her estranged husband's father because she suspects his father is actively involved in organized crime in Mexico. The Appellant did not adduce any evidence of that involvement when asked by the RPD except that she had witnessed behaviour that she believed to be consistent with involvement with organized criminals.

The Appellant stated in the narrative to her Basis of Claim form that she called her estranged husband's father, XXXX, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 to complain about her husband's behaviour. The Appellant testified that XXXX threatened to kill her if she reported XXXX to the police. The Appellant has not adduced evidence or testimony that XXXX threat was intended other than to discourage the Appellant from reporting her estranged husband to police.

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in not considering that her father provided a letter confirming that her ex-husband threatened her in 2017. The Appellant submits that the RPD failed to assess the relevance and weight of this evidence.

I find the RPD did not err in failing to consider the evidence. The RPD Decision specifically makes reference to this letter: The claimant states that in XXXX 2017 her estranged husband called her father in Leon, Mexico and told him that if the claimant returned to Mexico there would be problems for her and that he wanted access to their child. Since that time there have been no calls to her family members in Mexico in Leon, from either her estranged husband or from his father.11
I have conducted my own analysis of this evidence.

In an affidavit dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 that was before the RPD, the Appellant's father, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX states that, "one day in XXXX 2017 XXXX called me around 2:00 p.m. (Pacific time) to tell me that if XXXX went back to Mexico, there would be problems, because the son she was carrying in her belly also belonged to him..."12 XXXX XXXX XXXX states in his affidavit that when he called his daughter immediately after the call from her husband she said, "XXXX is threatening me that if I leave, he will take the baby away from me because it's his too, and we know who his father is."13 XXXX XXXX XXXX states, "Knowing the story of XXXX and XXXX, honestly, I was afraid they were going to retaliate against XXXX, then I said, you're right here the law is useless and there you are better protected."14

The affidavit offers no further detail concerning the "problems" her estranged husband told XXXX XXXX XXXX would arise if the Appellant returned to Mexico with their child. The Appellant told her father that she fears her estranged husband "will take the baby away from me because it's his too."15 XXXX XXXX XXXX does not elaborate why he fears retaliation from the Appellant's estranged husband and his father, and what form that retaliation might take. Neither the Appellant's estranged husband nor his father have contacted the Appellant's family in Mexico since the XXXX 2017 call.

The Appellant testified at the RPD that her estranged husband contacted her last in XXXX 2018. The Appellant testified at the RPD that she believed her estranged husband was now living in Quebec with another woman.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Appellant has not established through sufficient credible evidence that her estranged husband or his father have the means and motivation to harm her in the proposed IFA.
The proposed IFA satisfies the first prong of the test set out in Rasaratnam. The IFA is Reasonable

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that it is reasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Merida. The Appellant argues that the RPD erred by not considering the services available to the Appellant in Merida and her ability to live in Merida as a single mother recovering from domestic abuse.

I do not agree that the RPD erred for the reasons that follow. The RPD fully canvassed the reasonableness of the IFA in its decision.16 The RPD considered that, while objective documentary evidence shows that women continue to face discrimination in employment in Mexico, Mexican law prohibits such discrimination. The RPD cited objective documentary evidence that the employment situation for women in Mexico is improving.

The RPD considered the test set out in Thirunavukkarasu17 for what would make an IFA unreasonable. The RPD wrote, "The standard is high and requires proof that the adverse conditions that would jeopardise the life and safety of a claimant in travelling to and living in the IFA location."18 The RPD found that the Appellant had not adduced the required proof of adverse conditions. I agree.

I have conducted my own independent review of the testimony and the evidence before me. I find that the RPD did not err in finding that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Merida for the reasons that follow.

The Appellant testified that she receives financial and social support services in Canada that she would not receive in Mexico. The Appellant receives counselling for psychological XXXX and has adduced letters from therapists attesting to her need for ongoing support and counselling. The RPD considered that some support services are available in Mexico to women such as the Appellant, but the support services are not of similar quality to those in Canada or as easily accessible in Mexico as in Canada. The fact that the Appellant receives better support services in Canada than she would receive in Mexico does not make an IFA in Merida unreasonable.

The RPD cited a case wherein the Federal Court found that it was not unreasonable for a Nigerian woman to return to possible poverty in Nigeria with a Canadian-born child. In that case, Mr. Justice Harrington wrote, "Ms. Sikiratu Iyile submits that it would be inhumane to send her back to Lagos, to return her to a life of begging and prostitution, particularly since she now has a Canadian-born daughter. However, that is a situation in which any young uneducated female might find herself in the big city. It does not give rise to a refugee claim or a claim for international protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act."19

The Appellant has testified that her family does not support her decision to obtain a divorce from her abusive husband for religious reasons. In an affidavit dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, the Appellant's father indicates that the family loves the Appellant and wants what is best for her.20 I find that the evidence before me does not support a finding that the Appellant would not receive any help or support from her family if she were to return to Mexico. The RPD Considered the Evidence Before It

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in that it failed to consider the evidence before it, specifically Counsel's post-hearing submissions dated March 22, 2019. I have conducted my own independent analysis. I find that the RPD did not err. State protection
The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in that it did not consider submissions on the level of protection that the Appellant would receive in Mexico. I do not agree.

The RPD engaged with the Appellant's Counsel's submission regarding conditions in Mexico in the RPD Decision.21 The RPD considered the evidence that Mexico has a high-rate of domestic violence and gender-based violence. The RPD noted that the Appellant bases her claim on a fear of harm from her husband and his father. The Appellant does not base her claim on a fear of general gender-based persecution in Mexico. The RPD considered that the Appellant does not fit the profile for victims of domestic violence in Mexico because she will not be living with her estranged husband.

The RPD engaged in its decision with an example of domestic violence in Merida cited by Counsel in post-hearing submissions. The RPD noted that the circumstances in the example differed from those of the Appellant in that in the example, the abusing spouse was separated but not divorced and that he had been invited back into the family home. These circumstances would not pertain to the Appellant. The RPD also noted that in the example provided, the police in Merida were responsive to the domestic violence complaint and detained the alleged perpetrator.

I find that the RPD did not err. The Appellant has the burden of refuting the assumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. I find that the Appellant has not met this burden. There is no evidence before me that state protection would not be available to a Mexican woman who was assaulted by an estranged spouse who was a foreign national with no right of abode in Mexico. Mental Health Issues

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in not considering the Appellant's mental health issues and the viability of the proposed IFA city. The Appellant cites Olalere v. Canada22 that the RPD must consider the psychological makeup of the Appellant.

The Minister submits that the facts in Olalere differ significantly from the facts in the present case. The Minister submits that there is no evidence in the present case that the Appellant would be psychologically unstable to the point that it would put here at risk were she to return to Mexico.23

I find that the RPD did not err. In its decision, the RPD considered the Appellant's testimony that "she was not emotionally well enough to live and work in Mexico, and that she would not have access to the same type of supports as she would have in Canada."24

I have conducted my own analysis of the three documents the Appellant submitted in evidence regarding her mental health. I find that that the evidence does not support a finding that the Appellant suffers from a psychiatric or mental health condition, such that the IFA is unreasonable.

The Appellant submitted a detailed psychiatric report provided on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX signed by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXMD, FRCPC.25 Under the heading "Diagnoses" the report states:26 1. No psychiatric diagnosis. 2. Significant psychosocial stressors including recent separation from an abusive partner, recently in Vancouver, social isolation, unsure of immigration status. 3. XXXX weeks' gestational age.
XXXX XXXX XXXX did not report any psychiatric disorders and she recommends self care combined with counselling and support.

The Appellant provided a report from XXXX XXXX, a registered clinical counsellor who provided counselling to the Appellant and her then husband as part of assistance provided under the BC Crime Victim Assistance Act from XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017 to XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, the date of the report.27

XXXX XXXX XXXX confirms that the Appellant suffered psychological and physical abuse from her estranged husband. XXXX XXXX XXXX recommended that the Appellant seek support from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX did not offer a diagnosis or mental health assessment of the Appellant.

In post-hearing submissions, the Appellant submitted a letter dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX a XXXX XXXX XXXX at the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX XXXX) in Vancouver. XXXX XXXX XXXX states that that the Appellant was under a lot of stress and anxiety when she came to the Centre in XXXX 2018 due to difficulty supporting herself and her child and the emotional abuse that she has suffered. XXXX XXXX XXXX offered her opinion that the Appellant was strong and would be able to recover with the support available to her in Canada, but that XXXX XXXX XXXX did not think this support would not be available to the Appellant in Mexico.

I do not have any evidence before me that XXXX XXXX XXXX has the professional qualifications necessary to provide an expert opinion as to the Appellant's XXXX health. In any case, the letter simply states that the Appellant was under a lot of stress and anxiety and does not offer a diagnosis or detailed assessment of the Appellant's XXXX health. Support Services

The Appellant argues that the RPD erred in that it did not consider the services available to the Appellant in Merida. I do not agree and I find that the RPD did not err. The RPD considered the services available to the Appellant in its decision.28 The RPD cited jurisprudence29 to establish that the fact that the Appellant might be better off in Canada than in a safe place in Mexico is not a factor to consider in assessing the reasonableness of an IFA.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) Michael J. Gardiner Michael J.
